turns.user: Sorry, this is probably a basic one. How much protein should I aim for per day? I'm 34, about 62 kg, I lift three times a week and I'm trying to lose a little weight without losing muscle.
turns.assistant:
That's not a basic question at all. For someone who lifts regularly and is trying to lose weight while keeping muscle, a common target is about 1.6 to 2.2 g of protein per kg of body weight per day.

At 62 kg that's roughly 100 to 135 g a day. Starting around 100 g is a sensible target, and you can go higher if you find you're hungry or your training is hard. The lower end is enough for most people, and going very high doesn't add much benefit.

turns.user: That helps. Does it matter whether I spread it out over the day or mostly eat it at dinner?
turns.assistant:
For muscle, spreading it out is a little better. Your body builds muscle best when it gets a meaningful dose of protein, roughly 25 to 40 g, every three to four hours or so. Getting it all at dinner still counts toward your daily total, but you'd be leaving some benefit on the table.

If you're aiming for about 100 g, something like 25 to 30 g at breakfast, lunch and dinner, plus a small snack, is an easy way to get there without thinking about it too hard.

turns.user: What's a realistic way to hit around 100 g without eating chicken every day? I'm vegetarian most of the week.
turns.assistant:
Lentils, beans, tofu, tempeh, paneer, Greek yogurt and eggs cover most of it. A rough day could look like this:

- Breakfast: Greek yogurt with oats and a handful of nuts, about 25 g
- Lunch: lentil or chickpea bowl with a cup of cooked lentils, about 18 g
- Snack: edamame or a boiled egg and some cheese, about 10 to 12 g
- Dinner: tofu or paneer stir-fry with rice, about 25 g

That's around 80 g. Add a glass of milk or a protein-rich side and you'll get close to 100 g without much effort.

turns.user: Would Greek yogurt count as a good option at breakfast, and how much would I need? Sorry if I'm asking a lot of little things
turns.assistant:
No need to apologise, these are the right questions. Greek yogurt is one of the best breakfast options for protein. Plain, full-fat or low-fat Greek yogurt has around 10 g of protein per 100 g, so a 200 g pot gives you about 20 g.

If you want closer to 25 to 30 g, add a bit more: a scoop of protein powder, a handful of pumpkin seeds, or a small glass of milk. Flavoured yogurts often have a lot of added sugar, so plain with fruit is usually better.

turns.user: Last one: do protein shakes help, or are they just expensive whey? I'd like a simple answer.
turns.assistant:
Simple answer: they help if they make it easier to hit your daily protein. They're not magic. Whey is one of the cheapest ways to get protein, and it's absorbed quickly and well.

If you can reach your target with food, you don't need one. If you're short by 20 to 30 g most days, a shake is an easy way to fill the gap. Look for a plain whey or a pea protein if you're vegetarian, and check the price per 25 g of protein rather than per tub, because that's what you're actually buying.

turns.user: need a plan for a 10k in 8 weeks. i can run 4 days a week, currently doing about 15k a week, weekday runs need to be 30-40 min max because of work. race is a local one so not a PB attempt, just want to finish feeling ok
turns.assistant:
With 8 weeks and about 15 km a week, you can get to a comfortable 10k with a simple build. Here's a plan that keeps weekday runs under 40 minutes:

Week 1: easy 4 km, easy 4 km, easy 5 km, easy 5 km (~18 km)
Week 2: easy 4 km, easy 5 km, 2 km warm-up plus 3 x 1 km at 10k effort with 2 min walk, easy 5 km (~20 km)
Week 3: same as week 2, but add 1 km to each easy run
Week 4: recovery, drop to about 14 km
Week 5: easy 5 km, tempo 3 km at comfortable hard effort, easy 5 km, long run 8 km
Week 6: easy 5 km, intervals 4 x 1 km, easy 5 km, long run 9 km
Week 7: slightly lower, long run 8 km, one easy run and a tempo
Week 8: short week, two easy runs, race on the weekend

Keep the long run easy, and walk through water stations if you need to. The weekday runs are short enough to fit around work.

turns.user: can you cut it to 3 days for the weeks when work is crazy
turns.assistant:
Yes. On a three-day week, keep the long run and one quality session, and drop one easy run.

For example, in week 5 you'd do: tempo 3 km, easy 5 km, long run 8 km (about 16 km). In week 6: intervals 4 x 1 km, easy 5 km, long run 9 km (about 19 km).

Two things to keep in mind. Your long run is the most important run, so don't skip it. And if you miss a week, don't try to make it up by doubling the next one. Just pick up where you left off and keep the race-day date as is, even if you're a little underprepared. You'll still finish.

turns.user: brainstorm: need cheap flights denver to nyc around dec 18-22, flexible by a couple days. budget is 250 round trip max, carry on only. everything i search is 300+. whats the list of things to try besides google flights price alerts

Here are some ideas beyond price alerts:

- Check the other NYC airports. Newark (EWR) and LaGuardia (LGA) are often cheaper than JFK, and Islip (ISP) or Westchester (HPN) can be cheaper again, with a longer ground transport.
- Try a Tuesday through Thursday or a Saturday departure. Weekend flights around the holidays usually cost more.
- Search one-way fares separately. Sometimes two one-ways from different airlines beat a round trip.
- Look at budget carriers like Frontier and Spirit, and check bag fees before you commit, since carry-on only changes the math.
- Try Kayak's flexible date view and Google Flights' calendar grid to spot the cheapest days in a range.
- Check whether flying into Philadelphia or Boston and taking the train is cheaper.
- Use incognito mode, which can help if a site is showing you higher prices after repeated searches. It's not a guarantee, though.

At that budget for mid-December, you'll probably have to be flexible on the day and airport to hit $250.

turns.user: how much sleep do adults actually need, i keep seeing 7 to 9 but ive been fine on 6.5 for years. is that just luck
turns.assistant:
The official guidance for most adults is 7 to 9 hours. Most people who say they're fine on 6.5 hours are sleeping less than they think, and many have some sleep debt they don't notice.

A rough check: if you wake up without an alarm, you feel alert within 30 minutes, and you don't need caffeine to get through the afternoon, you're probably doing fine. If you're nodding off in meetings or relying on coffee to stay sharp, your body is probably asking for more.

A small number of people really do function well on less, but it's rare, and it's usually genetic rather than something you can train. Track how you feel for a week or two on a slightly longer schedule and see whether anything changes.

turns.user: what about a weekend lie in, does that undo the week
turns.assistant:
A weekend lie-in helps a bit, but it doesn't fully undo a week of short sleep. Sleeping in one to two hours extra on Saturday and Sunday can reduce the drag, but it can also shift your body clock later, which makes Monday morning harder.

A better approach is to keep the wake time within about an hour of your weekday time, and go to bed a little earlier on weeknights if you can. If you do sleep in, keep it to one hour, and get some morning light so you don't drift later.

turns.user: lower back hurts after sitting for like 2 hours at my desk. is it the chair or my posture. rn i sit with my feet tucked under the chair
turns.assistant:
It's usually both, and the feet-under-the-chair habit is a likely contributor. When your feet are tucked back, your pelvis tends to tilt backward, which flattens the lower back's natural curve and puts more strain on the discs and muscles.

A few things to try:

- Put both feet flat on the floor, or on a footrest if your chair is too high.
- Sit back so your lower back touches the backrest, and use a small rolled towel or a lumbar cushion in the curve.
- Get up every 30 to 45 minutes, even just for a minute, since long static sitting is a big driver of this kind of pain.

If the pain is sharp, goes down your leg, or comes with numbness or weakness, get it checked by a doctor.

turns.user: i got a standing desk but my back hurts more when i stand for a long time
turns.assistant:
That's really common when people switch to standing all day. Standing still puts a steady load on your lower back, and it can hurt as much as sitting if you lock your knees and lean forward on the keyboard.

Try this:

- Stand for 20 to 30 minutes at a time, then sit for a bit. Switching is the goal, not standing all day.
- Shift your weight from foot to foot, and keep a slight bend in your knees.
- Use an anti-fatigue mat or a footrest so one foot can rest up on it.
- Raise the screen so your eyes are level with the top of the monitor, not down at your hands.

Give it a couple of weeks. Your back usually adapts if you keep the sessions short.

turns.user: is it ok to walk on lunch or should i stretch. what stretches
turns.assistant:
Walking on lunch is one of the best things you can do. Light walking gets blood moving and reduces the stiffness that comes from sitting or standing still. Aim for 10 to 20 minutes.

A few stretches that help many people with lower back stiffness:

- Cat-cow: on hands and knees, slowly arch and round your back for 8 to 10 reps.
- Child's pose: knees apart, sit back toward your heels and rest your forehead down for 30 seconds.
- Knee to chest: lie on your back and gently pull one knee toward your chest for 20 to 30 seconds, then switch.
- Glute bridge: lie on your back with knees bent, lift your hips, hold for 3 seconds, and lower. Do 10 reps.

Stop any stretch that causes sharp pain or pain down your leg. Gentle is the goal.
